title: Who buried Moses?
summary: Deuteronomy says of Moses “he buried him” and that no man knows the grave. The verse does not name the one who buried him. Jude speaks of a dispute between Michael and the devil “about the body of Moses” and does not say what the dispute was or who buried the body.
text: KJV Deuteronomy 34:5: “So Moses the servant of the Lord died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the Lord.” KJV 34:6: “And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day.” KJV 34:8: “And the children of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days” KJV Jude 1:9: “Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses” Hebrew (WLC) Deuteronomy 34:6: וַיִּקְבֹּ֨ר אֹתֹ֤ו בַגַּיְ֙ [and he buried him in the valley]; וְלֹֽא־יָדַ֥ע אִישׁ֙ אֶת־קְבֻ֣רָתֹ֔ו עַ֖ד הַיֹּ֥ום הַזֶּֽה [and no man has known his burial place to this day]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 34:6: Καὶ ἔθαψαν αὐτὸν [and they buried him]. Greek New Testament (TISCH) Jude 1:9: διελέγετο περὶ τοῦ Μωϋσέως σώματος [he disputed about the body of Moses]. The Textus Receptus text served spells the name μωσεως; the other words are the same. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/5/34/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/DEU34.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/65/1/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/65/1/.
reasoning: The burial of Moses is told in one clause with an unnamed subject, and the verse adds that the place is unknown. Who carried out the burial bears on how the unknown grave is to be understood: a burial by the people who then mourned thirty days would be expected to leave a known grave, and a burial by God would not. The verse gives the valley and its neighbourhood and still says no man knows the sepulchre.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verse states: that “he” is the Lord, the last one named in verse 5; that the singular verb has an indefinite subject, “one buried him”, which is how the plural of Brenton’s Greek can be taken; that Moses was buried by an angel, a reading that draws on Jude 1:9. Jude does not say that Michael buried Moses. Check made: a search of the packaged KJV for verses that have “Moses” together with “buried”, “bury”, “sepulchre” or “body” finds Jude 1:9 and Numbers 9:6, and Numbers 9:6 is about another matter (Deuteronomy 34:6 does not repeat his name and is not found by that search); the twelve verses of Deuteronomy 34 were read in the KJV and none names a burier. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked passages do not explicitly settle who buried Moses. A published record that cites these verses concerns the writing and keeping of the law and the narrator’s later standpoint; this record asks only about the burial. The Greek plural is a separate G record. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry. The Greek New Testament wording is Tischendorf’s eighth edition as served by bolls.life (TISCH), compared with the Textus Receptus text served there (TR); neither is a critical apparatus.

title: The sun, moon and stars “divided unto all nations” — divided to them for what?
summary: Israel is warned not to worship the sun, moon and stars, “which the Lord thy God hath divided unto all nations under the whole heaven”. The verse does not say for what purpose they were divided to the nations. The next verse sets Israel apart: “But the Lord hath taken you”.
text: KJV Deuteronomy 4:19: “shouldest be driven to worship them, and serve them, which the Lord thy God hath divided unto all nations under the whole heaven” KJV 4:20: “But the Lord hath taken you, and brought you forth out of the iron furnace, even out of Egypt, to be unto him a people of inheritance” KJV 17:3: “either the sun, or moon, or any of the host of heaven, which I have not commanded” KJV 29:26: “For they went and served other gods, and worshipped them, gods whom they knew not, and whom he had not given unto them:” KJV Genesis 1:17: “And God set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth,” Hebrew (WLC) Deuteronomy 4:19: אֲשֶׁ֨ר חָלַ֜ק יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֶ֙יךָ֙ אֹתָ֔ם לְכֹל֙ הָֽעַמִּ֔ים תַּ֖חַת כָּל־הַשָּׁמָֽיִם [which the LORD thy God has apportioned, them, to all the peoples under all the heavens]. WLC 29:25, which is KJV 29:26: אֱלֹהִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא־יְדָע֔וּם וְלֹ֥א חָלַ֖ק לָהֶֽם [gods whom they did not know and he had not apportioned to them]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 4:19: ἃ ἀπένειμε Κύριος ὁ Θεός σου αὐτὰ πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσι τοῖς ὑποκάτω τοῦ οὐρανοῦ [which the Lord thy God has assigned, them, to all the nations under heaven]. 29:26: οὐδὲ διένειμεν αὐτοῖς [nor did he distribute to them]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/5/4/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/5/29/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/DEU04.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/DEU29.htm.
reasoning: The clause stands inside a warning against worshipping the heavenly bodies, and gives as a fact about them that God divided them to all nations. What was given to the nations — the use of their light, or the bodies as what those nations serve — changes what the passage says about the worship of other peoples. The same Hebrew verb is used at 29:26 (WLC 29:25) of gods “whom he had not given unto them”, said of Israel.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verse states: that the heavenly bodies were given to every nation alike for light and for marking time, as Genesis 1:17 says they were set “to give light upon the earth”, so that the clause is a reason not to worship what serves everyone; that they were allotted to the other nations as what those nations worship, while Israel was taken as the Lord’s own people (4:20), which is how the shared verb at 29:26 can be taken. The second reading does not by itself mean that such worship is approved. Check made: Deuteronomy 4:15–20, 17:2–5 and 29:24–28 were read in the KJV, and the Hebrew and Greek of the clauses quoted were compared; no other passage was searched, so a statement of the purpose elsewhere is not excluded. These checked passages do not explicitly settle for what the host of heaven was divided to the nations. The Hebrew of chapter 29 is numbered one verse lower than the KJV. No H or G is proposed. title: Moses blesses “the children of Israel” tribe by tribe — why is Simeon not named?
summary: Deuteronomy 33 is introduced as the blessing with which Moses blessed the children of Israel, and it names the tribes one after another. Simeon is not named in the chapter. The chapter gives no reason, though Simeon is named among the tribes six chapters earlier.
text: KJV Deuteronomy 33:1: “And this is the blessing, wherewith Moses the man of God blessed the children of Israel before his death.” KJV 33:6: “Let Reuben live, and not die; and let not his men be few.” KJV 33:7: “And this is the blessing of Judah” KJV 27:12: “These shall stand upon mount Gerizim to bless the people, when ye are come over Jordan; Simeon, and Levi, and Judah” KJV Genesis 49:5: “Simeon and Levi are brethren” KJV Genesis 49:7: “I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel” KJV Joshua 19:1: “their inheritance was within the inheritance of the children of Judah” KJV Numbers 1:23: “of the tribe of Simeon, were fifty and nine thousand and three hundred” KJV Numbers 26:14: “These are the families of the Simeonites, twenty and two thousand and two hundred” Hebrew (WLC) Deuteronomy 33:1: אֲשֶׁ֨ר בֵּרַ֥ךְ מֹשֶׁ֛ה אִ֥ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים אֶת־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל [with which Moses the man of God blessed the sons of Israel]. 33:6: יְחִ֥י רְאוּבֵ֖ן וְאַל־יָמֹ֑ת [let Reuben live and not die]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 33:6: Ζήτω Ῥουβὴν, καὶ μὴ ἀποθανέτω, καὶ ἔστω πολὺς ἐν ἀριθμῷ [let Reuben live and not die, and let him be many in number]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/5/33/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/DEU33.htm.
reasoning: The heading says the blessing is of the children of Israel, and the chapter then speaks of Reuben, Judah, Levi, Benjamin, Joseph with Ephraim and Manasseh, Zebulun, Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali and Asher. One of the tribes numbered in the wilderness and placed on mount Gerizim in chapter 27 has no saying. Whether that is a judgement on the tribe, a statement about its standing at the time, or an accident of the text changes how the chapter is read, and the chapter does not say.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the chapter states: that Simeon is passed over because of what Jacob says of Simeon and Levi in Genesis 49:5–7, though Levi is blessed here; that Simeon is counted within Judah, in whose land the tribe later has its inheritance (Joshua 19:1); that the tribe had become small, as the two numberings quoted may suggest; that a saying for Simeon has dropped out of the text. Check made: a whole-word search of the 29 verses of Deuteronomy 33 in the packaged KJV finds each of the other names listed above and does not find “Simeon”; the same search of all Deuteronomy finds “Simeon” at 27:12 only; the 29 verses printed on the cited page of Brenton’s Greek for chapter 33 were searched for the name and it was not found. That is a word search of the editions named, not a survey of manuscripts. These checked passages do not explicitly settle why Simeon is not named. The record does not claim that the blessing is defective or that it conflicts with another passage. No H or G is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original.
